Getting the Job Dung.

By: John Webb | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Could a species of insect, well known to us here in Africa, prove a secret weapon in the battle for a more sustainable future?

Unique Selling Point:
Dung Beetles don't get the publicity they deserve! For 60 million years they have toiled under a blazing sun, ridding the landscape of somebody else's mess. That "somebody else" is the bovine species we know as the cow: a voracious consumer of grass and depositor of poo. This insert will explain why that's not always good news for the environment and why countries as far afield as Australia and New Zealand are turning to dung beetles to undo the damage.

Summary:
One cow produces about 30kg - roughly equivalent to an average 7-year-old boy – of manure every day. There are about 10 million head of cattle in New Zealand, for example, equating to – give or take a pat or two – 300 million kg of dung per day. Multiply that several hundred times over and you have a poo problem of sizable proportions.

Now, that might not sound like bad news given our penchant for lathering our own gardens with organic fertilizers but an excess of nitrogen-rich manure is bad news for our rivers and oceans - where much of the dung ends up - and doubly bad news for water absorption in a rain-scarce country like South Africa.

Enter the humble dung beetle. If dung removal were an Olympic Sport, these guys would be the Jamaican relay team. They build tunnels up to 20cm beneath the soil's surface and fill them with dung. That has benefits which make everyone - farmers, environmentalists, governments and the beetles - a winner. Who would have thought, in this world of mounting crises and shrinking solutions, this particular problem would have a deployment-ready army, itching to do battle in the fight against dung? Another example of working with nature to help save nature.


Enter the humble dung beetle

Script:


VO1: A Dung Beetle walks into a bar. He says to the bartender: “excuse me, sir, is this stool taken?”

VO2: It’s easy to see why these creatures are the, (clear throat), butt of bad jokes but what’s less obvious is how they might help solve a problem that is no laughing matter. (PAUSE)

VO3: There seems no end to the pressure our planet is under right now, so forgive us for highlighting another crisis that often goes overlooked – one that might just surprise you.

VO4: You see, the world has a dung problem. The U.K. alone produces enough cow waste each year to fill their tallest skyscraper close to 80 times over. The Dutch dairy industry has an issue so big it’s been warned to drastically reduce its herd. Scientists describe it as a major environmental and health challenge – another one!

Link: Between one and one-and-a-half billion cattle in the world, each producing about 30kg of manure a day. Add in other livestock and animals and by 2030 it’s estimated the world will be producing 5 billion tonnes of dung every year. Now that's a lot of poo!

VO5: Much of that waste comes from intensively farmed livestock, and if you can’t use the dung or dispose of it efficiently, the impacts are potentially catastrophic. In concentrated amounts, it releases harmful greenhouse and other gasses into the atmosphere and threatens precious water resources.

VO6: Despite good news being as hard to come by these days as a pair of open-toed shoes in lockdown, we’re happy to say help is at hand!

Link: Enter the humble dung beetle. Now, if dung removal was an Olympic sport, they would be the Jamaican relay team!

VO7: And cheering them on would be entomology professor, Marcus Byrne: dung beetle aficionado and the reason we find ourselves at an urban park popular with dog walkers.

Marcus Byrne Uspound 00016 [01:01 – 01:07] So, what I’m going to do is dig all these guys out. It’s something I love doing. It’s like being a kid.

VO8: Some are rollers, others are tunnellers or dwellers – and most are eaters. Whichever way they choose to deal in dung, millions of years of practise have made them pretty darn good at it.

Marcus Byrne Upsound 00010 [00:48 – 00:50] That’s the eye there…

VO9: Masters of manure they may be, but surely that’s a look only a mother could love?

ITV Marcus Byrne [00:03:44:08 - 00:04:01:02] (include puff at start of answer) so much about their biology, um, is beautiful (CUT) [00:04:47:03 - 00:05:16:05] literally their eye structure, their wing structure, their body shape, their behaviour, the ability to orientate with celestial cues. You know, they are endlessly fascinating

Question Derek Watts [00:06:44:21 - 00:06:52:04] I'm sure you like a lot of different insects, but do you have a secret passion for the dung beetle?

ITV Marcus Byrne [00:06:53:10 - 00:07:06:05] (LAUGHS) That’s a difficult question. I think I have to admit, yes, I do, because, you know, they are so tenacious.

VO10: Tenacious AND resourceful. Prof Byrne was on a team that discovered these primitive looking beetles rely on the Milky Way to navigate when they fly. They use the bright strip of light generated by our galaxy to orientate themselves and move in a line relative to it. Their appetite for waste is just as impressive.

ITV Marcus Byrne [00:06:01:03 - 00:06:35:20] STRAP “Professor of Entomology: WITS” a big elephant, can produce 150 kilograms of dung in a day. Where's that dung? It’s gone and it's because these guys can shift this stuff at an incredible rate. (CUT) They can shift that in a couple of hours.

VO11: By comparison, a cow’s 30 kilos a day seems a little feeble. But, as many places in the world have discovered, that’s more than enough to ensure the - you know what – has hit the fan.

Link: As the world comes to terms with its dung crisis, there are some people hard at work trying to dig us out of this mess. One of them is an expert with a South African connection who’s developing quite a reputation in dung circles in New Zealand.

ITV Shaun Forgie [00:27:24:17 - 00:27:34:00] I'm probably considered the dung specialist – LAUGHS.

Forgie stills into laptop cutaways – Text on Forgie interview: “Recorded Earlier”

VO12: Kiwi entomologist, Dr Shaun Forgie, studied dung beetles at Pretoria University, but he’s now a man on a manure mission back home. Something we thought might interest Prof Byrne.

ITV Shaun Forgie [00:02:41:22 - 00:03:15:01] STRAP “Director: Dung Beetle Innovations” when it comes down to sustainability and farming. We're not sustainable in what we do here (CUT) And a large process of that could in my opinion be the result of not having a complete picture of our pastoral ecosystem.

VO13: The first cattle arrived in New Zealand in the early 1800’s – good news for meat and dairy lovers. Sadly, the humble dung beetle was left behind – bad news for the environment. As Doc Forgie says, the cows arrived without the clean-up crew.

ITV Shaun Forgie [00:03:45:11 - 00:04:16:03] so we've kind of modified things quite drastically here and the only thing we left out was introducing a part of that system which would be the recycling process which is largely down to the activities of dung beetles.
Cow gv’s into Prof Byrne looking at the laptop – audio of interview faint in the background

VO14: There are now around 9 million cows producing more than 80 million tonnes of manure each year – a scenario repeated in many parts of the world. In the absence of dung beetles, the soil is robbed of nutrients, harmful gasses are released, and, in a country as wet as New Zealand is, rivers risk pollution from run-off.

Marcus Byrne Upsound 00035 [00:03:08 – 00:03:27] I’m always nervous to talk on behalf of farmers but (CUT) most farmers learn their craft from their father, so it’s an inherited behaviour that we now need to leave behind.

Forgie stills and cell phone vid

VO15: And that’s exactly what Doc Forgie is trying to convince farmers to do. Through his Dung Beetle Innovations business, he’s aiming to retrofit a missing piece of the puzzle; getting them to introduce efficient communities of beetles onto their land to bury - and munch their way through - this toxic build up.

ITV Shaun Forgie [00:15:41:09 - 00:15:56:18] It's extraordinary when you see the the the sheer amount of manure that's getting relocated beneath the pasture surface it just makes me really really proud of dung beetles full stop when I see what they do. (Time Lapse here)

VO16: While caution when introducing exotic species is advisable, the process, says Doc Forgie, can be frustratingly slow. But he’s nothing if not dedicated.

ITV Shaun Forgie [00:27:34:05 - 00:27:38:10] I figure if I can fix this country and that's really what my objective is (CUT) I'm going to do it one way or the other, and the best way is with dung beetles.

Link (00050): South Africa can’t really be compared to New Zealand – not only because we play better rugby – but because we get far less rain. That creates a different set of challenges – both for us and for dung beetles.

ITV Mary Scholes [00:10:45:24 - 00:11:07:22] New Zealand doesn’t suffer from a water situation. New Zealand suffers essentially from a biodiversity situation and a very large number of livestock per unit area.

VO17: And by biodiversity, WITS professor, Mary Scholes, of course, means more than just the – uhm - feline variety. Thankfully, it’s not a situation we find ourselves in - despite the unrelenting pressure on natural habitats.

ITV Mary Scholes [00:12:40:17 - 00:13:12:13] STRAP “Professor: Animal, Plant and Environmental Sciences: WITS” there are all sorts of things that can utilize the dung, one of which is beetles (CUT) there are also all sorts of things like ants and termites, which we are very fortunate to have all that biodiversity in South Africa to deal with all the dung that is produced.

VO18: But a water scarcity situation we do have - you might say we’re Less Dung and More Dusted. But, we have 800 dung beetle species doing what they can to limit the impact on our soils by burying precious nutrients and keeping the ground porous as they go. Whichever way you look at it, it’s an impressive CV. And did we mention they control flies and could also help rehabilitate disused coal mines? Not bad for a creature so often overlooked.

Question Derek Watts [00:18:39:01] maybe we forgot the importance of the little things like the dung beetles and paid the price?

ITV Mary Scholes [00:18:50:08 - 00:18:55:17] Well, we hopefully have not yet paid the price (CUT) [00:19:16:14 - 00:19:22:10] It's the little things that are going to make sure that the system continues to hold (CUT) [00:19:23:06 - 00:20:05:14] I always play a game with my students, three of them together standing next to each other, they all have to stand on one leg and hold their palm up on either side. And if one of them fails, the system fails (CUT) that's what will happen if little things like dung beetles (CUT) are no longer functional in the ecology as we know it.

VO19: Saying our goodbyes, it was clear this story was about more than dung and the beetles that love it. It was about how nature - and a better understanding of it – holds the key to overcoming many of our environmental challenges. But every campaign needs a face, right?
Question Derek Watts [00:12:33:22 - 00:12:43:16] How do you see dung beetles as being maybe the poster insects of (CUT) working with nature rather than against it?

ITV Marcus Byrne [00:12:56:04 - 00:13:09:18] I think it would be a brilliant poster child because look at them, you can pick them up, they don't bite, they don't sting, they’re endlessly entertaining. They are fascinating in every aspect of their biology and they just do good things – what could be better?

ENDS.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Could a species of insect, well known to us here in Africa, prove a secret weapon in the battle for a more sustainable future?
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Dung Beetles don't get the publicity they deserve! For 60 million years they have toiled under a blazing sun, ridding the landscape of somebody else's mess. That "somebody else" is the bovine species we know as the cow: a voracious consumer of grass and depositor of poo. This insert will explain why that's not always good news for the environment and why countries as far afield as Australia and New Zealand are turning to dung beetles to undo the damage.
metadata.Summary: One cow produces about 30kg - roughly equivalent to an average 7-year-old boy – of manure every day. There are about 10 million head of cattle in New Zealand, for example, equating to – give or take a pat or two – 300 million kg of dung per day. Multiply that several hundred times over and you have a poo problem of sizable proportions. Now, that might not sound like bad news given our penchant for lathering our own gardens with organic fertilizers but an excess of nitrogen-rich manure is bad news for our rivers and oceans - where much of the dung ends up - and doubly bad news for water absorption in a rain-scarce country like South Africa. Enter the humble dung beetle. If dung removal were an Olympic Sport, these guys would be the Jamaican relay team. They build tunnels up to 20cm beneath the soil's surface and fill them with dung. That has benefits which make everyone - farmers, environmentalists, governments and the beetles - a winner. Who would have thought, in this world of mounting crises and shrinking solutions, this particular problem would have a deployment-ready army, itching to do battle in the fight against dung? Another example of working with nature to help save nature. Enter the humble dung beetle
